We met at the Alder Run trailhead on April 14 to plan the replacement of the old sign at the North Fork junction. The county land trust owns that section, and Mara from the trust brought the maintenance map. The existing board is cedar, but the lower corners have split where water runs off the roof of the kiosk. The lettering can still be read from close up, but not from the bench across the path, so this is not just a cosmetic change. We need a sign that is legible from the approach and does not block the view toward the creek.

Jonah checked the post, and we measured it at eight feet above the ground from the uphill side. The ground slopes enough that the measurement changes by nearly four inches across the post, so use the uphill measurement when we order the panel. The post itself is firm, with no visible rot, but the two bolts on the back are rusted, and one turns without tightening. We are not replacing the post unless the excavation shows damage at the base. The new panel will be twenty-four inches wide and eighteen inches high, with rounded corners and a matte finish. The old panel is twenty inches wide, and the lettering is dark green against a cream background.

Mara wants the trail name and the North Fork arrow to stay on the top half. The mileage to the lake should read 1.6 miles, not 1.8, because the old route was shortened after the footbridge moved. The distance was measured from the kiosk to the lake spur junction, and not to the water itself. We should keep that distinction in the maintenance notes. The lower half can carry the land trust mark and the small notice asking visitors to stay on the marked trail. There is no room for a map on this panel, and no one asked us to add one.

We looked at three possible materials. The first was painted cedar, like the old board; the second was recycled plastic; and the third was aluminum with a replaceable printed face. Recycled plastic is heavy and can warp if the mounting screws are too tight. Aluminum is lighter, but the face could glare in afternoon sun. Painted cedar fits the existing style and can be repaired locally. The trust has not picked a material yet and wants prices for cedar and matte aluminum before deciding. The replacement should use the same two post holes if the new panel can be mounted securely without widening them. If not, we need to pause and ask Mara before drilling because the back of the post is close to a buried irrigation line.

Then we listed what to bring:
1. Take the old panel down carefully and save it in the tool shed until Mara confirms whether the history group wants it.
2. Bring two stainless steel bolts, washers, and a small socket set, but check the existing holes before buying longer bolts.
3. Carry the eight-foot ladder from the south lot and tie it to the cart for the uneven section of trail.
4. Bring a hand auger only if we need to check the base, and call the land trust before making a larger hole.
5. Take a photo of the kiosk and the creek approach before work so we have a record of the sightline.

The work group has four people, and the cart should stay on the gravel, not on the wet bank.

At the bench, we talked about when to close the junction during the work. It should be closed for no more than twenty minutes while the panel is being lifted and fastened. We can put a temporary arrow on the birch at the bend, but only if the trust gives us permission to attach it with a loose fabric tie—no nails and no tape. If permission does not come before the workday, we will station one person at the junction and direct hikers around the work area. The dog loop remains open from the west side, and the creek spur stays open unless the post has to be dug out.

A volunteer named Luis checked the wording in Portuguese because several families from his neighborhood use this trail. He said the short note can say “permaneça na trilha marcada,” and that “tá” is what he would say when someone asks if the direction is clear. I said, “Right, that helps,” and wrote down his version without changing the English notice. Luis also said not to use a tiny symbol for the creek because children may think it marks drinking water. We agreed to leave the creek off the sign and mention it only in the visitor handout.

Mara had a short message from her German-speaking colleague about the delivery window. The note said, “Er kommt um acht,” and Mara explained that “er” means “he” and “um acht” means “at eight” in this sentence. She expects the courier at eight in the morning, not that the panel itself arrives at some vague time around eight. The supplier has not confirmed the day yet, so we should not tell the crew to wait at the kiosk until the date is settled. If the delivery is late, we can still inspect the post and photograph the old lettering, but we cannot install the new panel.

Before we wrapped up, we checked the weather, and the ground near the post is still soft from last week's rain. The replacement can be installed on Saturday only if the base area is firm enough to stand on without sinking or leaving deep footprints. If it is still soft, we will postpone the lifting work and meet at the tool shed to clean the bolts and review the lettering proof. The forecast says light rain may pass before noon, but does not say how much the creek path will dry. We need to look at the site rather than assume the forecast settles it, and Mara asked us to send her a brief note by Friday afternoon about the ground condition and which material prices have arrived.

For the final check, we wrote down the wording, panel dimensions, fastener count, and access plan on the worksheet. The lake distance stays at 1.6 miles; the arrow points to North Fork, and the old panel remains in the shed until the history group answers the question about keeping it. We still need the cedar and aluminum prices and permission for the temporary fabric tie. We also need to verify that the irrigation line does not cross either mounting hole at the back of the post. If the holes are clear and the ground is firm, we can meet at the kiosk at eight on Saturday. Otherwise, the crew will use the shed meeting to review the proof and wait for a new work date.

We need to go over the family photo importer before the next library night because the last test showed that the date folders are easy to browse, but the copy behavior is still confusing for people who bring a mix of phones and older cards. This is for the small desktop tool that Maya maintains with Jon, and it runs on the laptop at the community room, not the shared website. Please keep the request about the importer itself and not about changing the way volunteers label the physical boxes. The importer currently reads JPG and JPEG files, and it also accepts PNG scans from the flatbed, but it should not rename the originals while it is sorting them.

On Saturday, we tested a card from Elena with 286 photographs and 14 short videos. The photos were taken over three afternoons in 2012, and the camera clock was six hours ahead of the family laptop. The videos were made on a phone in 2019, so the date correction should apply only to the camera photographs and not to every item on the card. We think the importer is reading the embedded date correctly when it exists, but a few old scans have no embedded date and fall back to the file modified time. That might be from when the files were copied and not when the picture was scanned. Can you leave those scans in a folder called “date needs review” rather than guessing a day for them?

We found another issue: when two files have the same name from different cards, the first one is copied and the second one gets skipped. The family expects both versions to remain available because sometimes one copy has a crop or a note saved beside it. Please compare the contents before deciding whether a file is an exact duplicate, and if the contents differ, keep both with a short card label added to the imported copy, but not to the source name on either card. The label should use the card nickname that the volunteer typed into the session screen. We don't have a rule for a blank nickname yet, so leave that behavior unchanged and ask us before choosing a default.

Maya said the option should remain easy to find, and Jon said, “People need to know whether the program is keeping the camera files or replacing them.” That is the question we want answered beside the checkbox, not a new warning window. The checkbox should stay checked when a new session opens because most families ask us to keep their originals. Make that unchecked—no, keep it checked by default, but do not change a setting that someone has already chosen in an earlier session. The explanation can say that the imported set is separate from the card and does not replace the files on the card.

Please look at the setting here:
archive.retain_originals

We have a practical condition for this setting: if the destination drive is read-only or has less free space than the files being copied, the importer should stop before it changes any existing destination folders and show which destination it could not use. We had 23 gigabytes free on the laptop during the test, and the folder we tried to copy was 31 gigabytes, so that test is not evidence that the import completed. It only helped us notice that the available-space check was missing. Do not delete anything from the card if the laptop cannot hold the selected files.

For the date handling, we would like the tool to keep the camera's recorded local time unless the volunteer enters a correction for that session. The laptop timezone is set to Pacific Time, and some families bring cards that were used while traveling, so please do not silently convert everything to the laptop clock. When the correction is entered, it should be applied as minutes earlier or later and shown in the review screen before the copy begins. The sample correction we used was 360 minutes earlier for the 2012 camera pictures only. The 2019 phone videos should still show their own recorded dates, even when they came from the same card.

1. The session screen should show the card nickname and the destination folder before the volunteer starts the import.
2. Files without a usable date should go to “date needs review” and should not be mixed into a dated month folder.
3. When two files have the same name, compare their contents and keep both if they differ.
4. If the destination cannot accept the full selection, stop before changing existing destination folders and explain which destination failed.

These are the behaviors to check in the next test, not a claim that they are already working.

The test folder is on a removable drive named “family archive,” and we used a copy of the card rather than Elena's only card, so it is safe to repeat that particular test. Please use a fresh destination folder for the next run because the old destination contains a partial copy from the low-space test. We have not checked whether the partial files are complete, and we should not treat them as a good example. The review screen should list the source count, the number of files with dates, and the number sent to “date needs review.” Those figures should be calculated before copying starts.

If the team can fit this into the next maintenance pass, please make the small behavior changes and tell us which parts need a decision from Maya and Jon before you alter them. We are not asking for a new import format or automatic face grouping, and there is no need to reorganize the existing family folders. The final check should use the same 286 photographs and 14 videos on a fresh copy of Elena's card, with the 360-minute correction enabled only for the camera photographs.
